newsitem.title: UK: Country comes to London to defend hunting rights.
newsitem.headline: Country comes to London to defend hunting rights.

text.p: A rural army, angry and determined, converged on London's Hyde Park on Thursday to defend the centuries-old sport of hunting foxes and deer from extinction by Britain's new Labour government.

Tens of thousands of farmers, gamekeepers, aristocratic landowners and hunters have turned country communities into ghost towns with a show of strength which organisers hope will match a famous 1930s march by unemployed men to London from Jarrow in northern England.
The target of country dwellers' wrath is a parliamentary bill by Labour MP Michael Foster, due to be debated in November, which would ban the hunting of foxes, deer, hares and mink with dogs.

Hunting has roused strong passions in recent years with saboteurs often disrupting the activities of the red-jacketed huntsmen whose pursuit of foxes across field and dale with cries of tally-ho has inspired British writers for generations.
Members of parliament are being offered a free vote, a rarity used to decide issues of conscience such as the reintroduction of capital punishment.

But with Prime Minister Tony Blair supporting a ban and the newly-elected Labour government commanding a thumping 179-seat parliamentary majority, Foster's bill is probably the gravest threat that fox hunting has ever faced.
Foster denounces hunting as a "cruel and barbaric practice which should have ended centuries ago along with cock-fighting, bear-baiting and dog-fighting".

"They are trying to defend the indefensible. We are going to close the door on animal cruelty in this country," Foster told the BBC. Full-page advertisements in British newspapers on Thursday placed by an animal welfare group claimed seven out of 10 Britons wanted hunting with hounds abolished.

Hunt supporters see the bill, the latest round in a centuries-old town versus country battle, as the work of meddling urban do-gooders who would not recognise a fox if it bit them and know nothing of the role hunting plays in preserving the balance of nature.

The Countryside Marches and Rally, a coalition of sportsmen and women plus people employed in the countryside, say that rural pursuits provide employment for some 90,000 people and attract more than four million participants. They claim 13,000 hounds may have to be killed if hunting is banned.
Hundreds have walked to the capital from as far afield as the Lake District in the north and Cornwall in the south-west.

Dressed in yellow T-shirts bearing slogans such as "Give Country Jobs a Sporting Chance", the men and women who have spent three weeks on the road want to demonstrate that hunting is not merely a jolly sport for a few privileged landowners.

"Hunting plays such a significant role in the management of wildlife, no other method of control is so selective," said Robin Hanbury-Tennison, one of the organisers. "I would submit that all other methods can, when in the wrong hands, be extremely cruel."

The marchers have encountered nothing but encouragement on their walk to Hyde Park, seized from the church by Henry VIII in the 16th century to satisfy his demand for more hunting grounds, where they will be supported by many Conservative politicans including the party's new leader William Hague.

Britain's strong animal rights lobby has so far watched silently from the sidelines and several groups who regularly indulge in hunt sabotage have urged their supporters to stay away from Thursday's rally.

They are making their views known through a 1.5 million signature petition protesting at the killing of animals for entertainment which is being presented to Prime Minister Tony Blair's official Downing Street residence on Thursday.
